posts.content_md:
Hello,

I seem to have accidentally procured an old research Nd:YAG laser as well as an Ar-ion and a few spare Nd:YAG frames. Problem is, I am a bit out of my league with using them, and am hoping for some advice.

The YAG is a Spectra Physics something or another (I can probably look at the model number tomorrow), and is powered by Xenon flashlamps and a power supply the size of a small refrigerator (the caps in that thing are awesome!). It is frequency doubled, and includes all the optics to clean up the beam and spit out a green and IR line (532/1064 nm)

I don't have the specs or datasheet for the laser, but it is labelled as 130 W. I find this very odd, because it's a pulsed laser. I would expect a pulsed laser to give me the energy per pulse, not the power, because the average power is going to depend on how many times I pulse it per second.

Does anyone have any experience with what this might mean? Our best guess is that it's designed to run off the power supply at one rate, and at that rate it's spitting out 130 W.

In any case, I'd really like to use this sucker for flash holography. I've got some VRP-M film from integraf lying around from some attempts to use our smaller 100 mW Ar-ion laser (this totally failed, the thing was air cooled and we never got an image- any ideas for fixing the problem would be great, but I think it's just not good enough for holography).

Does anyone have any experience using this sort of laser for holography? How do we find out what sort of protective eyewear is necessary? How do we find out if optical equipment we buy for beam expanding is good enough to not explode? Will this thing just catch the film on fire?

The Ar ion is an 8 W CW water cooled unit- we're not sure if it works yet, but we'd want to use it for the same application, though flash holograms probably aren't as doable. Any advice for dealing with it would be much appreciated =)

Thanks,

-Brian

posts.content_md:
Brian, set up an interferometer with the Air Cooled Ion laser. It will tell you everything. Start off with path lengths of each leg being the same length. Monitor the fringes.

As far as the pulsed laser, if it is pumped by Xenon flash lamps then it is pulsed. Does the power supply have different pulse rates, ie. 1 PPS. 5 PPS, 50 PPS etc? If so it may be the wattage is a function of the higher pulse rate but, and may be be a caculation based on the raw IR energy without doubling and cleaning. But this is just a guess based on my experience working with pulsed YAG lasers (not for holography). Is the pulsed laser head water cooled? I think it would be. Look at the head for inlet out oulet water connections. We used objectives and simple glass lenses for our high power pulsed laser but the objective has to be the ones that do not have optical adhesives within them (this blackens on high power). For a pinhole, high power pinholes are available. Depending on wavelength used one can purchase, Gold plated, Molybdenum, Tungsten, ceramic and even Diamond pinholes. For puled holography, which is using a single pulse, you would need to determine the energy per pulse first then you can spec out the optics required.

Eyeware can be purchased easily (do a search on the interenet - even eBay) and is decided on by the output wavelength.

> **JohnFP:** As far as the pulsed laser, if it is pumped by Xenon flash lamps then it is pulsed. Does the power supply have different pulse rates, ie. 1 PPS. 5 PPS, 50 PPS etc? If so it may be the wattage is a function of the higher pulse rate but, and may be be a caculation based on the raw IR energy without doubling and cleaning. But this is just a guess based on my experience working with pulsed YAG lasers (not for holography).

It looks like the laser is actually constant output, what I originally thought were "flash lamps" were actually "arc lamps". Is this worse for holography? It seems like I want a single high power pulse, not a constant beam.

It does seem to have a large amount of optics, including what looks like a "Q switch" and a frequency doubler. I'm not quite sure what a Q switch is, but for some reason I'm thinking this can be used to make pulses... or am I confused?

Oh, and looking at the optics reveals something totally sweet -- there's not just a green output, but a purple one as well!

> **JohnFP:** Is the pulsed laser head water cooled? I think it would be. Look at the head for inlet out oulet water connections.[\quote]Yes, definately water cooled. It's pretty neat looking at how the mechanism works, it looks quite simple and elegant. Basically, there's a 208 3-phase input at 30 A, which is transformed up to 220 V. This goes into a control board and straight to the arc lamp (nice, maximum of 6600 watts of power being dumped into the Nd:YAG crystal).The cavity itself is a elliptical prism, with the arc bulb at one focii and the crystal at the other. There's a piece of glass between the two sides, I'm guessing to protect the crystal. The arc bulb fits exactly in the length of the cavity, and you just connect the power leads from the supply directly to the ends of the bulb -- elegant.Meanwhile, a water pump pumps water over the bulb and crystal to cool and recirculates through a deionizer. It seems likely that the piece of glass between the two sides of the ellipse is also to promote laminar water flow. It looks like the water is pumped back up to the control cabinet (roughly the size of a small refrigerator) where there's a heat exchanger. It doesn't look like this gets connected to an outside water source, but I haven't turned it on yet (need to install the 3-phase outlet).As far as actual hologram production goes, I'm planning on starting with some green sensitive silver emulsion from integraf or something (I've forgotten where I ordered it from), and then making my own DCG. I'm a Material Scientist, so I've got some decent equipment to coat glass with, and Alfa seems to have no problems shipping Ammonium Dichromate to me. Lucky =) Now I just need to find a source for some dyes to increase green sensitivity (any recommendations? I've read that Rhodamine 6G is good, but that information is almost a decade out of date by now).In any case, thanks for the information, it's been very helpful =)

Uhh... watch out, that purple output is probably 260-something nanometer light. Very heavily UV, if I remember correctly. (I think the human eye normally only goes down to 350 or 400nm. I should really look these things up before posting about them...)

If you can see it, that means there's probably so much output that you seriously need protective eyewear!

That's a heck of a find though. If you want to convert it to pulse output, you might want to ask on alt.lasers...

posts.content_md:
> **meekan01:** It does seem to have a large amount of optics, including what looks like a "Q switch" and a frequency doubler. I'm not quite sure what a Q switch is, but for some reason I'm thinking this can be used to make pulses... or am I confused?

A q-switch is basically a very fast optical switch. It's generally used in pulsed lasers to concentrate the energy of the laser into a very short pulse, rather than a lower-peak-power wider one that would otherwise result.

If you have a q-switched laser with CW pumping of the lasing medium, you'll probably get a train of very fast high-power pulses that average to 130W. Kind of like PWM modulating the output of a chip to get an analog voltage...

To use it as a pulsed laser for holography, you want one single BIG pulse. I did a quick search on alt.lasers and came up with the following related thread:

[http://groups-beta.google.com/group/alt ... 17b267f4d3](http://groups-beta.google.com/group/alt.lasers/browse_thread/thread/cc8f28149757a25f/b7f1f217b267f4d3?q=lamps+xenon&rnum=1&hl=en#b7f1f217b267f4d3)

"1. CW arc lamps have very thin walls - below 1mm, more like 0.5mm 

This is in order to keep thermal resistance low. 

2. Flashlamps are much more thick-walled. The discharge acoustic wave 

is a big stress to envelope material. "

So you probably won't be able to use your existing arc-lamps for pulsed holography. (The laser might very well work for regular CW holography, however.)

But, you might be able to replace them. Please post to alt.lasers asking the professionals for advice before you try it on my say-so, I'm just a hobbyist!

[http://repairfaq.ece.drexel.edu/sam/COR ... 04-04.html](http://repairfaq.ece.drexel.edu/sam/CORD/leot/course04_mod04/mod04-04.html)

Judging by this page, you guys will probably need to heavily modify the power supply in addition to replacing the arc-lamp with a flash-lamp. Assuming you can find a lamp that fits appropriately in the cavity, the power-supply modification should be fairly simple. You already have the monster 1F demonstration array, this just bumps the voltages up a bit and adds some pulse-shaping
